Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original 0/Unknown score rested on no cited source. Located Guinea's Credit Bureau Law (L/2019/0056/AN, 30 December 2019) via the National Assembly archive, which requires prior authorisation from the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea (BCRG) before any credit database or backup site is relocated abroad, conditional on the host country offering equivalent or superior security guarantees — a sectoral data-localisation requirement for financial/credit data. Guinea's 2016 Cybersecurity and Personal Data Protection Law (L/2016/037/AN) covers data protection generally but does not impose a broad localisation mandate. Revised score to 3 (sectoral requirements only) rather than 0/Unknown.
revised_comments: Guinea imposes a sectoral data-localisation requirement covering credit bureau data. Under the Credit Bureau Law (Loi L/2019/0056/AN of 30 December 2019), any relocation of credit databases and backup sites outside Guinea requires prior authorisation from the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea (BCRG), granted only where the host country can guarantee security measures equivalent to or exceeding those provided in Guinea. Beyond this sector-specific rule, the 2016 Cybersecurity and Personal Data Protection Law (L/2016/037/AN) regulates personal data generally but does not mandate broad data localisation across other sectors.

revised_comments: Guinea's government operates a national data centre, certified Tier 3 by the Uptime Institute, inaugurated in Conakry in September 2025 to host government data and strengthen digital sovereignty. A January 2026 government sector review confirms the facility is operational alongside an expanded national fibre backbone and a newly operationalised internet exchange point.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original 0/Unknown score rested on no cited source. A World Bank project appraisal (2019, citing a 2016 household survey and 2017/2018 EDG tariffs) shows average household electricity spend at the subsidised tariff equal to roughly 1.2% of monthly household income (GNF 52,785 versus average monthly income GNF 4,401,589), rising to roughly 10.6% only under a hypothetical full cost-reflective tariff that consumers do not currently pay. A 2025 academic study of Guinea's PV market corroborates that EDG's progressive residential tariff remains very low (107-453 GNF/kWh, roughly USD 0.01-0.05/kWh), among the lowest in West Africa. Revised score to 4 (Affordable, 1-2% of income) based on tariffs actually paid by residential consumers. Flagged for human review because the underlying survey/tariff data are dated (2016-2019), no fresher affordability-specific study was located, and the subsidised-versus-cost-reflective framing materially changes the score (1.2% vs 10.6%).
revised_comments: Residential electricity tariffs in Guinea are low relative to income. The state utility Electricite de Guinee (EDG) applies a progressive residential tariff of roughly 107-453 GNF per kWh (approximately USD 0.01-0.05/kWh), among the lowest in West Africa. World Bank household survey data indicates that an average household spends around 1.2% of monthly income on electricity at the subsidised tariff actually charged, placing affordability within the 'Affordable' band, although this masks a far higher effective cost (over 10% of income) were tariffs raised to full cost-recovery levels, which they currently are not.
